title: Corky leaf blisters after humid nights
scenario: Small raised blisters appear mainly on the undersides of several leaves. Older bumps become tan and corky. The root zone has stayed wet overnight and nighttime humidity has been high, but the grower is preparing to spray for mites.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Mostly lower leaf surfaces

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Raised blisters becoming corky rather than fine feeding stipple

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: New lesions appeared after several humid, low-transpiration nights

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: No pest has been confirmed under magnification

question: What is the strongest next step before applying a pesticide?

options.label: Inspect both leaf surfaces with magnification and review irrigation, RH, and airflow history
options.rationale: This directly separates a physiological edema-like pattern from pests or infectious lesions while testing the moisture-balance context.

options.label: Spray immediately because any raised bump proves mite feeding
options.rationale: Raised lesions are not specific to mites, and an unverified spray can add phytotoxicity or obscure the original pattern.

options.label: Increase irrigation so the leaves remain fully hydrated
options.rationale: If water uptake is already exceeding water loss, more moisture can strengthen the leading physiological explanation rather than test it.

options.label: Remove every affected leaf before recording the pattern
options.rationale: Removing the evidence first makes it harder to compare lesion age, location, and response to corrected conditions.

differential: Edema or intumescence associated with water uptake exceeding transpiration
takeaway: Blisters and corky bumps are not automatically pests. Confirm the organism and reconstruct the water-transpiration context before choosing a control.

title: Twisted new growth near an air intake
scenario: New leaves become narrow, twisted, and cupped on plants closest to one intake. Several non-crop plants outside that side of the structure show similar distortion. No nutrient change occurred.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Strongest near one air intake and weaker farther away

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Newest tissue is narrowed, twisted, and cupped

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Symptoms appeared after nearby vegetation was treated

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: Multiple plant species show a similar spatial gradient

question: Which investigation most strongly tests an off-target exposure hypothesis?

options.label: Map affected plants against the intake and review nearby application and ventilation history
options.rationale: A multi-species spatial gradient tied to an exposure pathway is stronger evidence for drift or volatilization than leaf shape alone.

options.label: Increase micronutrients because the newest leaves are distorted
options.rationale: The spatial gradient and cross-species pattern are not explained by a whole-crop nutrient shortage.

options.label: Assume a virus because distortion involves new growth
options.rationale: Systemic pathogens remain a differential, but the exposure pattern should be tested before assigning a transmissible cause.

options.label: Ignore nearby non-crop plants because they are different species
options.rationale: Similar injury across species can be a valuable clue when investigating an environmental or chemical exposure event.

differential: Herbicide drift or volatilization entering through the intake
Microscopic mites or systemic disease as competing explanations
takeaway: Distribution is evidence. A gradient linked to an intake plus injury on multiple species can be more informative than trying to diagnose distorted leaves from shape alone.

title: Speckling after a foliar spray
scenario: Small pale and necrotic spots appear the morning after a foliar application. Spots are most concentrated on exposed upper leaf surfaces and resemble the droplet pattern from the spray.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Exposed sprayed leaf surfaces

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Discrete specks and small spots resembling droplet coverage

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Appeared soon after one documented application

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: No similar injury was present before the spray

question: What should be reconstructed first to separate phytotoxicity from disease?

options.label: The spray record, tank history, rate, mixture, and environmental conditions around application
options.rationale: The symptom timeline and droplet-like distribution make exposure history the strongest discriminating evidence before assuming an infectious process.

options.label: Apply the same mixture again to see whether the spots get worse
options.rationale: Repeating a suspected harmful exposure is not a safe diagnostic test and can compound injury.

options.label: Add more fertilizer because the spots contain dead tissue
options.rationale: Necrosis is an outcome shared by many injuries and does not establish nutrient shortage.

options.label: Diagnose a fungal leaf spot without checking lesion progression or magnification
options.rationale: Disease remains possible, but the event-linked distribution should be tested first.

differential: High-light or heat interaction with wet treated tissue
Leaf-spot disease or pest injury coinciding with the spray
takeaway: A precise timeline can be diagnostic evidence. When injury begins immediately after a spray and follows its coverage pattern, reconstruct the exposure before adding another treatment.

title: Bleached tops after a light increase
scenario: The highest leaves become pale and slightly curled several days after fixture output was increased. Lower and shaded leaves on the same plants remain greener.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Highest and most exposed canopy surfaces

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Paling and curl follow the light-exposure gradient

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Began after a documented fixture-output increase

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: PPFD and leaf temperature have not been remapped since the change

question: Which measurements most directly test the leading explanation?

options.label: PPFD and leaf temperature at affected and shaded canopy positions
options.rationale: These measurements test whether the visible gradient follows photon and thermal exposure rather than assuming the pale color is nutritional.

options.label: Only the nutrient label on the reservoir
options.rationale: The reservoir label does not explain why injury is concentrated at the most exposed canopy positions after a lighting change.

options.label: Only room air temperature at the wall
options.rationale: A remote air sensor can miss the leaf temperature and radiant environment experienced by the damaged tissue.

options.label: Increase feed strength before taking light measurements
options.rationale: Adding dissolved salts does not test the strongest timeline and spatial evidence.

differential: Canopy overheating interacting with high radiant load
Root-water limitation made visible first in the highest-demand tissue
takeaway: Bleaching that tracks fixture exposure should be measured as an exposure problem before it is interpreted as nutrient deficiency.

title: Fine stippling without webbing
scenario: Fine pale stippling appears on several leaves. There is no webbing, so the grower assumes spider mites are impossible and starts adjusting nutrients instead.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Scattered leaves with strongest injury near lower surfaces

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Many fine pale feeding-like points rather than uniform chlorosis

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: The stippled area is expanding over time

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: Leaf undersides have not been inspected with magnification

question: What is the strongest next step?

options.label: Inspect leaf undersides and symptom edges with magnification for mites, eggs, thrips, and pest signs
options.rationale: Webbing is not required for early mite infestations. Direct organism evidence is more diagnostic than either webbing absence or nutrient photo matching.

options.label: Rule out spider mites solely because there is no webbing
options.rationale: Webbing is generally associated with heavier populations and its absence does not exclude mites.

options.label: Increase nitrogen because the leaves contain pale dots
options.rationale: Fine stippling is not the typical evidence needed to establish a whole-leaf nitrogen shortage.

options.label: Wait until the whole plant is bronzed before scouting
options.rationale: Delaying direct inspection can allow a pest population to increase while early evidence is already available.

takeaway: Absence of webbing is not absence of mites. Use magnification and inspect the organism, eggs, fecal signs, and damage pattern directly.

title: Flower browning after condensation
scenario: A few dense flower clusters develop localized browning after several nights with high humidity and visible condensation. Surface tissue looks mostly normal from a distance.

observations.label: Location
observations.value: Dense flower interiors rather than the whole plant

observations.label: Pattern
observations.value: Localized internal browning and softening

observations.label: Progression
observations.value: Appeared after repeated high-humidity nights

observations.label: Known context
observations.value: The flower interiors have not been opened and inspected closely

question: What is the strongest next step?

options.label: Open representative affected flowers carefully, inspect internally with magnification, and review humidity/condensation records
options.rationale: Dense flower disease can progress internally before obvious surface sporulation, so direct tissue inspection plus microclimate history best separates mold from senescence or physical damage.

options.label: Assume normal senescence because the outer flower still looks acceptable
options.rationale: Surface appearance can miss internal decay, especially in dense tissue after persistent moisture events.

options.label: Mist the flowers to see whether the brown tissue softens
options.rationale: Additional wetting can increase disease risk and does not provide useful diagnostic separation.

options.label: Change root-zone fertilizer without inspecting the flower
options.rationale: A localized internal flower pattern after condensation is poorly matched to a whole-root-zone nutrient change.

differential: Localized senescence or dead embedded tissue
takeaway: Dense flowers must be inspected internally when rot is plausible. Environmental history and direct tissue evidence are more useful than judging the flower from its outer surface.
